name: Lena Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew in the mountains for the power company, and these days almost all our work is wildfire hardening. That means making the lines less likely to start a fire: swapping bare wire for covered conductor, putting sections underground through the canyons, fitting new switches that cut the power in a split second if something touches the line. I start at six with the weather and fire-risk forecast, and the AI on my phone pulls together the day's permits, the access roads and who's on shift. Then it's a lot of dust, steep slopes and a lot of checking that everybody's harness is on right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy that it matters. Five years ago a fire started from a line two valleys over and burned a whole town, so when we finish a section, I know we've made somebody safer. What wears me out is the permits and the heat. On weekends my husband Marco and I run a small training school, teaching pole climbing and safety to people who want to get into the trade, and I use the AI every day for the bookings, the course notes and the advertising. Marco says I'd marry the app if he let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, it's a useful tool and that's all it ever needed to be. Online I'd probably post something like, back to work, everyone. At church I'd say the good Lord gave us brains and hands, and we'll keep using both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plans carry on. I'd keep my crew going till sixty-two and build up the school with Marco. A plateau suits a small business just fine, nobody comes along and changes the rules on you every six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for the school, because it already saves me about ten hours a week on the admin. We'd probably buy a second training pole and a new set of harnesses next spring, maybe ten thousand all in. I'd keep investing a bit each month, like I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, settled. Like a good season with no surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the training school start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years ago Marco hurt his back and had to come off the poles, and he was going stir crazy at home. We had a field behind the house and some savings, so we put up two poles and started teaching on Saturdays. Now we've got a waiting list, and our daughter Sofia does the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still expand the school in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, slowly. Maybe add a course on underground cable work, because that's where the jobs are going around here. I'd do it carefully and pay for it out of what the school earns, no loans.

S0.say: She'd say AI is a useful tool and that's all it needed to be, posting that it's back to work. At church she'd say people were given brains and hands and will keep using both.
S0.think: She thinks her plans carry on: crew work until sixty-two and building up the training school. A plateau suits a small business because the rules don't keep changing.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for the school's admin, saving about ten hours a week, and plans to spend about ten thousand on a second training pole and new harnesses next spring. Keeps investing a little each month and considers adding an underground cable course paid from earnings, without loans.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like a good season with no surprises.
S0.quote: A plateau suits a small business just fine, nobody comes along and changes the rules on you every six months.
S0.fieldNote: Lena combines a senior crew role with a family training business, and uses AI every day to run it. She's traditional in faith and thrift, careful never to borrow, and entrepreneurial at the same time. Her pride in wildfire work comes from seeing a town burn two valleys over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how a free economy works, things change and people find new things to do. At work I'd say let's learn the new kit and stay ahead. Online I'd say people should stop waiting for someone to rescue them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd see an opportunity. Somebody has to train people to work alongside the robots and drones. If the trade is changing, I want my little school to be the place people come to learn the new version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a drone and sensor course at the school within the year, and I'd look at buying a used robotic arm for training, if I could find one for under forty thousand. At work I'd volunteer for any trials. I'd keep saving and investing as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit nervous about the money, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the school lose customers if robots took over tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the pole-climbing courses might shrink, yes. But the new courses would bring in different people, maybe older workers who need to retrain. You've got to follow where the customers are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think government should help people adjust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but mostly I'd want them to get out of the way. Make it easier for small businesses like mine to set up new training, and give people a voucher they can spend where they like, instead of building some big government programme. People and families should take the lead.

S1.say: She'd say that's how a free economy works: things change and people find new things to do. Online she'd say people should stop waiting to be rescued.
S1.think: She'd see an opportunity, since someone must train people to work alongside robots and drones. She wants her school to be where people learn the new version of the trade.
S1.do: Adds a drone and sensor course at the school within the year and looks for a used robotic training arm under forty thousand. Volunteers for trials at work and keeps saving and investing as normal.
S1.feel: Excited, a bit nervous about the money.
S1.quote: If the trade is changing, I want my little school to be the place people come to learn the new version.
S1.fieldNote: She treats steady change as a business opportunity and moves fast on it. Her free-market view comes through in wanting government to step back and offer training vouchers rather than programmes. She's willing to spend a large sum on a robot arm, but only if the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is very fast, and people need to get moving rather than complain. Online I'd post practical advice on how to retrain. At church I'd say families should look after each other and not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a shock even for me. I like change, but two years doesn't leave time for my school to change with it, and I've got thirty thousand tied up in poles and harnesses. I'd still be all right, but it would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop any new spending on the school and talk to Marco and Sofia about where it goes. I'd see if we could turn it into training for robot technicians, and I'd ask the company to let me help run the robot rollout on my crew. If the school didn't work out, we'd sell the equipment and put the money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than I'd show. I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the training school if robots can do the hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots can climb, people won't pay to learn climbing, simple as that. Maybe there'd still be people who want to work on the robots, or check their work. I'd try to pivot fast, but I'm honest enough to say I might lose that business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your son's a firefighter. How do you think about him in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He fights fires, which I think is one of the last things they'd hand to a robot, but I don't really know. He's thirty and stubborn like his mother. I'd tell him to save and learn whatever new equipment they bring in, and that we're here if he needs us.

S2.say: She'd say it's very fast and people need to get moving rather than complain, posting practical retraining advice. At church she'd urge families to look after each other rather than wait for government.
S2.think: Even she finds it a shock, because two years leaves no time for her school to adapt, with thirty thousand tied up in equipment. She'd be all right, but it would hurt.
S2.do: Freezes new spending on the school in the first month and plans its future with her husband and daughter, trying to pivot to robot technician training. Asks to help run the robot rollout on her crew, and sells the equipment and saves the money if the school fails.
S2.feel: Uneasy, more than she'd show, kept busy by doing.
S2.quote: I like change, but two years doesn't leave time for my school to change with it, and I've got thirty thousand tied up in poles and harnesses.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability is still there, but she admits the speed would beat her small business. She's frank that she might lose it. Her free-market outlook keeps her focus on personal and family responsibility rather than blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's get ahead of it. Online I'd post about the new courses we're running. At church I'd say get your family ready, learn something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a good amount of time. I could turn the school into something for the new world before it arrives. Five years is enough to retool a small business if you start on Monday, not next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the robot technician course by 2028, buy a training robot arm, and partner with a technical college if they'd have us. I'd take a short course in robotics myself. At work I'd help run trials and retire at sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, busy, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time let you do with the school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets us change slowly, test the new courses, and sell off the climbing kit while it's still worth something. In the fast one we'd be stuck with it. Here we'd have time to make the switch properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really for me. Maybe Marco, he's sixty-one and not as keen on change as I am. And I'd worry about people who wait too long, but you can't make people move if they don't want to.

S3.say: She'd say there are a few years to get ahead of it and post about new courses. At church she'd urge families to get ready and learn something new.
S3.think: She thinks five years is a good amount of time to retool her school for the new world before it arrives, if she starts straight away.
S3.do: Launches a robot technician course by 2028, buys a training robot arm and seeks a technical college partnership. Takes a short robotics course herself, helps run trials at work, sells the old climbing kit while it holds value and retires at sixty-two.
S3.feel: Calm, busy and a bit excited.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to retool a small business if you start on Monday, not next year.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for her to turn the school around, and she has a concrete plan with dates. She's less patient with people who wait too long, which fits her self-reliant outlook. Her husband's slower pace is a quiet contrast she acknowledges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse not to be ready. Online I'd post about how small businesses can prepare. At church I'd say teach your children to work hard and keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's comfortable. I'd retire from the crew and spend a few years running the school full-time. By the time the robots arrive, I'd like to be the one selling them the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start slowly: add a drone course next year, then sensors, then robots. I'd keep investing a bit each month and keep the school debt-free. I'd retire from the power company at sixty-two and work at the school after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start changing the school now, or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait a year or two, see what tools actually turn up, then move. With ten years, no need to rush and waste money. The worst thing you can do in business is buy the wrong machine too early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your grandchildren, if you have them, to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work hard, to pray, to save, and to keep learning new things. And that a trade is something to be proud of, whether it's climbing poles or fixing robots.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse not to be ready, and post about how small businesses can prepare. At church she'd urge parents to teach children to work hard and keep learning.
S4.think: She thinks it's comfortable for her: she'd retire from the crew and run the school full-time for a few years. By the time robots arrive, she wants to be the one selling the training.
S4.do: Adds courses to the school step by step, first drones, then sensors, then robots, after waiting a year or two to see which tools turn up. Keeps investing monthly and the school debt-free, then retires from the power company at sixty-two to work at the school.
S4.feel: Calm and looking forward to it.
S4.quote: The worst thing you can do in business is buy the wrong machine too early.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she becomes careful, waiting to see which tools arrive before spending. Her plan is to move from lineworker to full-time trainer in the new trade. Her values of faith, thrift and hard work sit comfortably alongside her love of new technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would leave my school stuck with the wrong kit and no time to change. What would help is fewer rules on setting up new training, and training vouchers people can spend at small schools like ours, so we can move fast and help people get new skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about fires. Whatever happens with robots, lines will still need to be safe in dry mountains, and someone has to check that. I hope whoever does it, person or machine, takes it as seriously as we do.

headlineQuote: By the time the robots arrive, I'd like to be the one selling them the training.
portrait: Lena Torres is a 58-year-old crew leader doing wildfire hardening in the mountains who also runs a weekend pole-climbing and safety school with her husband. She's traditional in faith, thrift and self-reliance, never borrows, and uses AI every day for the school's admin. She's calm or excited in the plateau and steady change pictures, seeing a chance to train people for the new trade. The two-year AGI picture makes her uneasy because her school wouldn't have time to adapt, while five and ten years let her retool it and plan to sell training for the robots themselves.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, because her training school would be stuck with the wrong equipment and no time to change.
whatWouldHelp: Fewer rules on setting up new training, and vouchers people can spend at small schools like hers so they can move fast.
